question: Vibe Coding a Turbine Blade
content: Blake Scholl describes how hardware engineering at Boom Supersonic traditionally worked — engineers passing Excel spreadsheets via email, no source control, no automated testing. AI changes this fundamentally.
description: You are a hardware engineering manager who just learned that your team's aerodynamicist and structures engineer have been exchanging a 50-MB spreadsheet over email for the past six months. According to Blake Scholl, what is the fundamental problem with this workflow?
options: The spreadsheet is too large for email servers to handle reliably
Hardware engineering workflows are treated as software but lack
Excel spreadsheets cannot handle the complexity of turbine blade design
The engineers should be using CAD software instead of spreadsheets
answer: Hardware engineering workflows are treated as software but lack
explanation: Blake Scholl explains that a lot of hardware engineering happens in Excel spreadsheets with VBScript — it's actually software, but treated as if it's not, with no source control or automated testing.

question: Two Engineers, One Jet Engine
content: Blake Scholl describes the new model at Boom Supersonic: software engineers create the architectures, and hardware engineers vibe-code their pieces. The result is a dramatic reduction in the team size needed for complex engineering.
description: Your VP of Hardware says you need a team of fifty engineers to design a jet engine from scratch — that's the industry standard. Based on Blake Scholl's experience at Boom, what counter-argument can you make?
options: Fifty engineers is actually the minimum because of FAA certification requirements
With software engineers creating architectures and hardware engineers vibe-coding,
You should outsource the engine design entirely to a specialized vendor
Fifty engineers is fine if you divide them across aerodynamics and structures teams
answer: With software engineers creating architectures and hardware engineers vibe-coding,
explanation: Blake Scholl says with the new model — software engineers creating architectures and hardware engineers vibe-coding their pieces — two engineers can design an entire jet engine.

question: The Human-in-the-Loop Hardware Simulator
content: Max Hodak describes moving from Excel to Python models for believable simulations of physical systems. He also predicts AI will soon generate STEP files and PCB layouts, not just software.
description: You run a hardware startup that relies on mechanical and electrical engineering simulations. Your team currently uses Excel for most calculations. Max Hodak sees a three-stage progression for AI in hardware. What is it?
options: Excel → Python simulations → AI generating
Manual drafting → CAD software → 3D printing
Spreadsheets → databases → cloud computing
Prototyping → testing → manufacturing
explanation: Max Hodak says he moved from Excel to Python models for simulations, and predicts AI will soon generate STEP files and PCB layouts — coming for mechanical and electrical engineering next.

question: Software Engineers Build the Scaffold
content: Guillermo Rauch reacts to Blake's description by noting a major shift in enterprise software: no startup can sell you hardware collaboration tools anymore because companies just build what they need internally.
description: A VC pitches you a startup that builds collaboration software for hardware engineering teams. Guillermo Rauch would argue this startup faces a fundamental problem. What is it?
options: The hardware engineering market is too small to support a SaaS business
Companies are now just internally coding exactly what they need, so there's no
Hardware engineers refuse to use any cloud-based software for security reasons
The startup would need ten years to build a product competitive with Excel
answer: Companies are now just internally coding exactly what they need, so there's no
explanation: Guillermo Rauch says there's no startup that builds hardware collaboration tools that can sell you anything anymore — internally, you're just coding the right thing you need at any given time.

question: Spreadsheets Are Lightweight Programming
content: Naval observes that spreadsheets with VBScript were successful because they approximated custom software — they were 'lightweight programming' for people who couldn't build real software.
description: A colleague argues that spreadsheets are simply data organization tools and have nothing to do with software engineering. Based on Naval's take, why did spreadsheets with VBScript become so dominant in engineering?
options: They were the only tools available for collaboration in the 1990s
They approximated custom software for people who couldn't build real software —
Microsoft Excel had a marketing advantage that crushed all competitors
Spreadsheets are inherently better than code for any type of engineering analysis
answer: They approximated custom software for people who couldn't build real software —
explanation: Naval says spreadsheets were successful because no one could build custom software, so a spreadsheet approximating custom software was the best available option — it was lightweight programming.

question: The Thousand-Blade Problem
content: Blake Scholl details the turbine blade design problem: a blade changes shape from cold to hot, requiring conversion between aerodynamics and structures. With a thousand blades per engine, manual iteration is infeasible.
description: Your team needs to analyze how each of the thousand turbine blades in a jet engine deforms under operating temperatures. Doing one blade manually takes an engineer a full day. What does the new AI-enabled workflow allow instead?
options: It automates the analysis so you can change blade geometry and see structures and
It eliminates the need for turbine blades entirely by using ceramic coatings
It lets one engineer analyze all thousand blades in a single day with zero errors
It outsources the analysis to a cloud compute cluster running legacy Fortran code
answer: It automates the analysis so you can change blade geometry and see structures and
explanation: Blake Scholl says with the new combination of software and hardware people, you can change blade geometry and see in real time the structures and aerodynamics results — a complete transformation from one-day-per-blade.

question: Agentic Hardware Interfaces
content: Naval suggests that hardware companies with historically bad software may skip human-facing software entirely and go straight to agentic interfaces — an agent accesses the hardware and you talk to it through voice.
description: A hardware startup building IoT devices asks you whether they should invest in building a polished mobile app or a web dashboard for their product. Using Naval's prediction, what alternative path should they consider?
options: They absolutely need a polished mobile app to reach consumers
They should build both a web dashboard and a mobile app for maximum coverage
They could skip human-facing software entirely and let agents access the
They should license their API to larger companies who will build the front-end
answer: They could skip human-facing software entirely and let agents access the
explanation: Naval says it 'may not even be software with a human front end — it might just be completely agentic, an agent accessing it, and you talk to it through voice to control hardware.'

question: You Always Want the Smartest Model
content: Naval argues that intelligence is an 'unalloyed good' — you always want more of it. When models make mistakes, you don't know it, and they're always cheaper than a real person.
description: Your CFO proposes using a cheaper, less intelligent AI model for 97% of coding tasks and only using the frontier model for the hardest 3%. Based on Naval's argument, what is the flaw in this cost-saving strategy?
options: The cheaper model costs more in compute than the frontier model
When the cheaper model makes a mistake, you won't know it, and intelligence is too
The cheaper model is actually more intelligent than the frontier model for coding tasks
The strategy would violate the AI model's terms of service
answer: When the cheaper model makes a mistake, you won't know it, and intelligence is too
explanation: Naval says: 'When these models make a mistake, you don't know it' — and intelligence is an unalloyed good. Given the leverage poured through decisions, you always want the most intelligent model.

question: The Two-Tier Model Strategy
content: Guillermo describes a practical split: use frontier models for pushing the coding frontier, and use cheaper models (including Chinese models and Gemini) for support tasks, browser automation, and industrial production.
description: You are designing an AI deployment strategy for your company. You need both cutting-edge code generation and cost-efficient automation for routine tasks. How does Guillermo Rauch suggest splitting the workload?
options: Use one model for everything to keep the architecture simple
Use frontier models for pushing the coding frontier and cheaper
Use only open-source models to avoid vendor lock-in across all tasks
Always use the cheapest model and accept lower quality for all tasks
answer: Use frontier models for pushing the coding frontier and cheaper
explanation: Guillermo says: 'Any time I'm working to push the frontier, you need the best possible coding model. That's basically two or three models. The Chinese are certainly not in it.' For other tasks, cheaper models work fine.

question: The Monopoly Problem
content: Naval acknowledges that his preference for the most intelligent model is 'not great news' because it concentrates power among the top two or three frontier labs, creating a monopoly or oligopoly situation in AI.
description: A policy maker is concerned about AI market concentration. You explain Naval's argument that everyone will gravitate toward the single most intelligent model. What market structure does this predict for AI?
options: A highly fragmented market with hundreds of competitive AI models
A monopoly or oligopoly where the top few frontier models dominate because users always prefer
A market where open-source models eventually beat proprietary ones through community contributions
A market where every company fine-tunes its own model and no single player dominates
answer: A monopoly or oligopoly where the top few frontier models dominate because users always prefer
explanation: Naval says: 'Which isn't great news, because it means you'll end up creating a monopoly or oligopoly situation in AI. But I always want the most intelligent programmer.'

question: The Intelligence Unicorn
content: Guillermo reveals that Chinese models are 'certainly not in it' when it comes to frontier coding — despite all the hype, the real frontier work is dominated by just two or three Western model providers.
description: A tech journalist claims 'Chinese AI models are now competing head-to-head with Western frontier models on coding tasks.' Based on what Naval and Guillermo agree on, is this claim accurate?
options: Yes, DeepSeek has surpassed GPT-4 on all major coding benchmarks
No — neither Naval nor Guillermo sees Chinese models being used for frontier
Partially — Chinese models lead on coding but trail on creative writing
The comparison is meaningless because Chinese models don't publish benchmarks
answer: No — neither Naval nor Guillermo sees Chinese models being used for frontier
explanation: Naval says he doesn't know anyone who uses Chinese models. Guillermo confirms: 'The Chinese are certainly not in it' when it comes to frontier coding. Chinese models find use in support and automation, not cutting-edge coding.
